name: Smilacaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach Smilax as the monocot vine that breaks the parallel-vein stereotype: woody/prickly climbing stems, paired petiolar tendrils, broad leaves with 3-5 strong veins and reticulate cross-veins, separate-sex 6-tepaled flowers in umbels, and berries.

project_scope.selection_mode: Smilax bona-nox + Smilax tamnoides project module
project_scope.note: Both species are accepted by current Kew and native-range treatments include Texas.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Find the paired tendrils at the petiole base, then look at the leaf veins. Smilax leaves have several strong longitudinal/arcuate veins but a visible net of smaller cross-veins—unusual for a monocot.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Perennial rhizomatous climbing vines or shrubs, often prickly. Leaves alternate, usually leathery, prominently 3-veined or 5-veined with reticulate cross-veins; tendrils usually arise from the petiole region.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Plants usually dioecious. Small greenish flowers are in umbels and have 6 tepals; staminate and pistillate flowers occur on separate plants.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Round berries, commonly black at maturity in the two project species, with 1-3 seeds.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Prickly climbing vine + petiolar tendrils + broad reticulate 3-5-veined leaf + umbel + berry = Smilacaceae/Smilax.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: tendril origin → reticulate monocot leaf → prickles → umbel/sexes → berry → bona-nox vs tamnoides
visual_lesson.intro: Greenbrier is a great monocot lesson because it looks 'too broad-leaved' to be one. The tendrils and 3-5 strong veins are easy to see, but the fine network between them is the surprise.

steps.title: 1 · Find the tendrils at the petiole
steps.look_for: Paired curling tendrils associated with the petiole/leaf base.
steps.why_it_matters: This is one of the fastest Smilax field characters.

steps.title: 2 · Prove the leaf is reticulate
steps.look_for: Three to five strong primary veins with a clear mesh of smaller cross-veins between them.
steps.why_it_matters: Breaks the misleading 'monocots always have parallel veins' shortcut.

steps.title: 3 · Read the separate-sex umbels
steps.look_for: Small 6-tepaled flowers grouped in round umbels; male and female flowers occur on separate plants.
steps.why_it_matters: Adds reproductive confirmation beyond prickles and tendrils.

steps.title: 4 · Saw greenbrier door
steps.look_for: Thicker often lobed/hastate leaves, broad cartilaginous marginal band, often stout flattened dark-tipped prickles.
steps.why_it_matters: Leaf margin/shape and prickle build distinguish it from bristly greenbrier.

steps.title: 5 · Bristly greenbrier door
steps.look_for: Thinner mostly unlobed leaves with basal margins minutely serrulate and conspicuous unequal flexible dark bristles/prickles on lower stems.
steps.why_it_matters: FNA identifies the flexible unequal bristles and basal serrulation as strong species clues.

steps.title: 6 · Confirm with black berries
steps.look_for: Round black berries held in umbel-like clusters.

comparisons.title: Smilacaceae vs ordinary dicot vine
comparisons.rule: Smilax may look dicot-like because of broad reticulate leaves, but it retains monocot flower architecture with 6 tepals and characteristic petiolar tendrils/major venation.

comparisons.title: S. bona-nox vs S. tamnoides
comparisons.rule: Bona-nox = thick often lobed/hastate leaf with cartilaginous margin + stout flattened prickles. Tamnoides = thinner mostly unlobed leaf + basal serrulation + flexible unequal bristles.

visual_lesson.caveat: Leaf shape in S. bona-nox is extremely variable even on one plant. Do not identify it from a single lobed or unlobed leaf; use margin texture, prickle form and multiple leaves.

genera.fast_cue: prickly climbing vine + petiolar tendrils + 3-5-veined reticulate leaf + umbels + berries
